summary: Specifies how peers use Kerberos version 5 technology under the Generic Security Service API, so applications can use Kerberos through the common programming interface. It is on the standards track as a proposed standard.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 1964 specifies how programs using GSS-API exchange Kerberos V5 authentication and protected data. It gives both sides common rules for the tokens, names, and credentials they use.

subtitle: How GSS-API peers use Kerberos version 5 tokens, names, and credentials.

tldr.problem: Applications using the Generic Security Service API need a shared definition for using Kerberos V5 as their security mechanism.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines context-establishment tokens, per-message integrity and wrapping tokens, name forms, credential handling, status values, and quality-of-protection values.
tldr.outcome: RFC 1964 is a Proposed Standard from June 1996 and has been updated by RFC 4121 and RFC 6649. It defines DES-based options and warns that its MD2.5 integrity algorithm may be weaker than DES MAC MD5.

today: RFC 1964 is a Proposed Standard published in June 1996. The unit metadata lists RFC 4121 and RFC 6649 as updates to it.

sections.title: Kerberos as a GSS-API Mechanism
sections.content:
RFC 1964 defines the protocol-visible parts of the Kerberos V5 mechanism for the Generic Security Service API (GSS-API). It specifies the tokens exchanged between peers for security-context setup, message protection, and context deletion, without defining the separate exchange between a GSS-API endpoint and the Kerberos Key Distribution Center (KDC).

The mechanism is identified by an Object Identifier (OID). The RFC gives the identifier used during experimentation and the identifier used after advancement to Proposed Standard.
sections.plainLanguage: GSS-API gives programs a common way to request security services. This RFC defines how that common interface works with Kerberos V5.

sections.title: Setting Up a Security Context
sections.content:
The initiator begins with a GSS-API InitialContextToken. Its inner token contains a Kerberos KRB_AP_REQ preceded by the two-byte token identifier 01 00. The same framing identifies other Kerberos messages: 02 00 for KRB_AP_REP and 03 00 for KRB_ERROR.

The authenticator includes a sequence number and a checksum that carries channel-binding information, context flags, and optional delegation data. The checksum type is 0x8003; its value is at least 24 bytes and includes a length, an MD5 hash of the channel bindings, and flags. Optional delegation data carries a forwardable ticket-granting ticket in a KRB_CRED message.

Without a mutual-authentication request, the target does not send a reply token. With mutual authentication, it replies with a KRB_AP_REP or KRB_ERROR; the AP-REP includes its optional sequence-number field.
sections.plainLanguage: The initiator sends a Kerberos request inside a GSS-API token. If it asks for mutual authentication, the other side sends a reply that lets the initiator confirm the exchange.

sections.title: MIC, Wrap, and Context Deletion Tokens
sections.content:
A MIC token is sent separately from user data and lets the receiver check its integrity. A Wrap token carries the data and its integrity information, with optional encryption. A context-deletion token is produced when the application deletes the security context.

The MIC token identifier is 01 01, the Wrap identifier is 02 01, and the deletion identifier is 01 02. Their headers identify the integrity algorithm and carry a sequence number and checksum. Wrap also identifies its sealing algorithm. Tokens have no embedded length field, so the application must frame them in its higher-level protocol.
sections.plainLanguage: A MIC travels beside the data and helps detect changes. A Wrap token carries the data with integrity protection and can also encrypt it.

sections.title: Checksums, Sequence Numbers, and Padding
sections.content:
The checksum covers the data with the first eight bytes of the token header logically placed before it. The defined integrity choices are DES MAC MD5, MD2.5, and DES MAC. The RFC says MD2.5 had limited evaluation and might be significantly weaker than DES MAC MD5; support for DES MAC might not be present in every implementation.

Each MIC or Wrap token carries an encrypted eight-byte sequence field. It combines the sender's four-byte counter with a direction indicator: zero for the initiator or FF for the acceptor. Receivers can use the value to detect replayed or out-of-sequence tokens, but providing those detection services is optional.

Wrap data is padded to a multiple of eight bytes, with an eight-byte random confounder prepended. When DES sealing is used, the padded data is encrypted with DES-CBC using a key derived from the context key.
sections.plainLanguage: Each protected message has a checksum and a sequence number. The sequence number helps distinguish messages from the two directions and can help detect replay, if the implementation provides that service.

sections.title: Names Accepted by the Mechanism
sections.content:
The mechanism defines mandatory name forms for Kerberos principal names, host-based service names, and exported name objects. A principal name has one or more components separated by / and may include a realm after @; a backslash quotes special characters in components and realms.

A host-based service name uses the form service@hostname. The hostname is looked up in DNS and replaced by the returned fully qualified name when available; it is mapped to lower case. If the lookup fails, the supplied hostname is used. The RFC also lists optional user, machine UID, and string UID name forms whose meanings depend on the operating system.
sections.plainLanguage: Names must use agreed formats so both programs interpret them the same way. The formats include Kerberos principals and services associated with host names.

sections.title: Credentials and Protection Choices
sections.content:
Initiating and accepting a security context use different Kerberos credentials. A client typically has a ticket-granting ticket and session key in a credentials cache. A service uses its service key, typically stored in a key table, to accept contexts. If the service needs initiating credentials and its key is in the key table, the mechanism should use that key to obtain a ticket-granting ticket from the KDC.

The RFC defines minor status codes and quality-of-protection values for integrity and confidentiality algorithms. Every implementation MUST accept input buffers of at least 16 Kbytes for the specified GSS-API calls and support the corresponding Wrap output in Unwrap.
sections.plainLanguage: Clients and services use different credentials when they start or accept a protected conversation. The RFC also sets shared error and protection values so applications can work across implementations.
